Reference real UIs (Football Manager player profile, Fight Night Champion, WHOOP/Hudl body maps) and say what to copy from each.

message.content:
**1. Body-wear figure: a stylised muscle map, front and back**

My pick is a flat, stylised muscle map in the style of sports-science apps, not a rendered MetaHuman body or a plain outline. Here's why:
- A muscle map reads its six regions as shapes. A rendered body at about 200 px tall turns into skin-tone mush with overlays floating on top, and it competes with the MetaHuman head render top-left, which is already the realism anchor.
- A plain outline has no inner areas to fill, so wear would only show as tinted outlines, which is weak at a glance.
- Flat vector panels can be tinted per region directly, need no render pipeline, and scale cleanly to 1080 and to a phone.
- Proportions are still traced from our own MetaHuman athletic male and female bodies in A-pose, front and back. That keeps the silhouette true to our fighters and gives the source a recorded origin. No MPFB, no stock anatomy art.

**Spec in the 480×420 panel**
- **Layout:** a 24 px panel title row and 24 px padding. The front and back figures stand side by side, each about 150×300 px with 40 px between them, centred, feet on a shared baseline. Small "FRONT" and "BACK" captions sit under the feet at 11 px, caps, 60% white.
- **Construction:** each figure is about 14 to 18 flat muscle panels grouped into the six regions. Head and neck, torso and core (chest, abs and obliques on the front; traps, lats and lower back on the back), arms (deltoid, biceps or triceps, forearm), and legs (quads or hamstrings, calf).
  - Panels are separated by 2 px gaps in the navy background colour, not by lines. That keeps it clean at small sizes.
  - The outer silhouette has a 1.5 px stroke at #2A3854.
  - The hands are simple mitts and the face is blank. The figure is a diagram, not a portrait.
- **Female variant:** the same panel set on the female MetaHuman proportions: narrower shoulders, a different waist-to-hip ratio and adjusted chest panels. The regions and colours are identical.
- **Left and right:** the regions are the fighter's own left and right. On the front view the fighter's left arm appears on the viewer's right. Put a tiny "L" and "R" at the shoulders, 10 px at 50% white, so nobody has to guess.

**The four wear colours on the navy (EXAMPLE values; check them against the S206 sheet)**

| State | Fill | Word |
|---|---|---|
| Pristine | #3A4A66 (cool slate, a quiet resting state) | PRISTINE |
| Fatigued | #C9A227 (our gold, muted) | FATIGUED |
| Degraded | #E07A2E (amber-orange) | DEGRADED |
| Critical | #D64545 (red, kept for the stoppage tier) | CRITICAL |

The fourth word, CRITICAL, is EXAMPLE because Kalli owns the words. Use three colours if the game only has three states.

State is never shown by colour alone:
- Every region carries its word and its %.
- Degraded and Critical regions also get a diagonal stripe at 12% opacity inside the panel. Use 6 px stripes, wide enough not to shimmer.
- Critical adds a small "!" in a circle on the panel.

**How a region shows DEGRADED**
- No pulsing or breathing animation; it's static.
- The region gets a 2 px inner stroke in its own colour, plus an outer glow of about 8 px blur at 35% opacity in the same colour, clipped to the figure.
- On hover, or when a label is selected, that region brightens by 15% and the others drop to 70%. It's a one-time change, not a loop.

**Where the % labels go**
- Six callouts sit outside the figures, three down the left edge of the panel and three down the right, connected by 1 px leader lines at #2A3854 that end in a 4 px dot on the region.
- Each callout is two lines:
  - The region name in caps, 11 px, 60% white, for example "LEFT ARM".
  - The value in the condensed sans, 18 px bold, in the state colour, then the word in caps, 11 px, for example "62%" then "DEGRADED".
- Put the arms and head on the shoulder side and the torso and legs lower down, so the leaders never cross the figure.
- Values come from the game. Any number in mocks is EXAMPLE.

**When every region is PRISTINE (the empty state)**
- The whole figure is in slate #3A4A66 with no glow and no stripes.
- The six callouts collapse into one line under the figures: "ALL REGIONS PRISTINE", 12 px caps, in gold. Under it, at 11 px, 50% white: "No wear carried from training or bouts" (EXAMPLE string).
- The figure stays visible, so the panel never looks broken. It looks like a clean medical card.

**2. The empty bottom-right panel: the weight-cut track**

I pick the weight-cut track over training milestones, sparring partners or a coach's note. It's the one thing a manager checks every week that has a hard deadline, it fills the space with a chart instead of text, and it ties straight to fight night.

Layout sketch for the panel below LAST 3 WEEKS (assumed about 480×420; match the actual panel):
- **Row 1, title (24 px):** "WEIGHT CUT" in 14 px caps gold, with the weight class on the right, for example "WELTERWEIGHT · 147 LB", at 12 px, 60% white.
- **Row 2, hero numbers (about 64 px), three columns:**
  - "CURRENT" with "152.4" at 32 px bold white.
  - "TARGET" with "147.0" at 32 px, 60% white.
  - "TO CUT" with "−5.4 lb" at 32 px, in a state colour (green on track, amber tight, red risky). It also gets a word ("ON TRACK", "TIGHT" or "RISKY"), never colour alone.
  - Labels are 11 px caps, 50% white. All numbers are EXAMPLE.
- **Row 3, the chart (about 200 px):**
  - A line chart of the last 6 weeks plus the weeks to the bout.
  - The actual weight is a 2 px white line with 4 px dots per weigh-in.
  - The planned cut is a dashed gold line from today to the weigh-in date.
  - The class limit is a thin horizontal line in slate, labelled at the right end.
  - Today is a vertical 1 px line marked "TODAY".
  - The weigh-in day is a vertical gold marker with a small scales icon.
  - The x-axis shows week labels at 10 px; the y-axis shows three values only.
- **Row 4, footer (about 56 px):**
  - On the left, "WEIGH-IN" followed by the date, and on the right "RATE NEEDED −0.9 lb/wk", both at 12 px.
  - One line from the coach at 12 px italic, 70% white, for example "Water cut last 48h only." (EXAMPLE string).
  - This absorbs the coach's note idea without giving it a whole panel.

With no bout booked, the chart shows the weight trend against the class limit only, with a footer line: "No weigh-in scheduled" (EXAMPLE).

**3. The bout-record panel with no bouts**

Replace the text with a record card that's real but empty, so the panel keeps the same shape it will have later.
- **Top row:** the record digits shown as "0 – 0 – 0" in the big condensed numerals (W–L–D), at 40 px, in 40% white, with "W", "L" and "D" captions underneath. Next to it, a "DEBUT PENDING" chip, in a gold outline with gold text at 12 px caps.
- **Middle:** three ghost rows in the exact layout of future bout rows: date, opponent, result chip and method. They're drawn as rounded bars at 6% white, with no fake data. This shows the shape the panel will fill into.
- **Bottom: a "PATH TO DEBUT" line from real game data.** For example: amateur record if the game tracks it, sparring rounds logged ("SPARRING 24 rds" EXAMPLE), the current readiness grade, and "NEXT: book a debut bout" as a gold text link that opens matchmaking.
  - If the game has none of that data, show only the 0–0–0 card and the chip. Don't invent filler.

**References and what to copy from each**
- **Football Manager player profile:** copy the dense, calm information hierarchy: small caps labels, big numbers, every panel filled, and the condition and injury readout as a body diagram with per-region status. FM also proves a flat figure works next to a real photo. I haven't checked the exact current-version layout of FM's injury diagram, so treat the specifics as NOT VERIFIED.
- **Fight Night Champion:** copy the boxing-specific damage idea: regions of the boxer marked as hurt between rounds, readable in a second. Copy the read, not the look, because ours is a calm management screen, not an in-fight overlay. The exact presentation of its damage screen is NOT VERIFIED from here.
- **WHOOP:** copy its strain and recovery language: one hero number, a state word, and colour bands on a dark background. That's the model for our callouts and the weight-cut hero row. I haven't checked whether WHOOP shows a muscle map; I'm citing it for its colour-state language only.
- **Hudl and sports-science body maps:** copy the flat muscle-panel body map, front and back side by side, with tinted regions and a legend. This is the figure style I picked. Which Hudl product, if any, shows one is NOT VERIFIED.

**What not to do**
- Don't put a rendered MetaHuman body in this panel: the head render already does the realism.
- Don't pulse or loop glows.
- Don't use teal for wear states; teal is UI only.
- No fine hatching under 6 px.
- No placeholder figures: every figure has to trace from our MetaHuman bodies, so the source is recorded.

I can mock this up as a 1920×1080 overview tab with both panels filled and send the PNG if you want to see it before Claude builds it.

Maria - art direction M45 (FightCamp, S235). Long, complete answer; do not cut it short.

The 3D boxing club (Godot 4, stylised realistic, bright and alive) has rooms off the training floor: office (wood panelling, parquet, red
brick outside), physio (white tiles, cold tub), reception (orange-tiled wainscot, checker floor). The camera looks DOWN into a room at ~55-65
degrees from a 3/4 angle. The operator marked our stills: the wall nearest the camera covers the room ("walls should be transparent"), a dark
slab fills the bottom of the frame, and doorways are bare gaps or a pale see-through panel ("door?", "add doors ?").
Art-direct, ready to build:
1. CUTAWAY: how the walls between camera and room should read - faded (what alpha), cut down to a stub (what height, how the cut top edge is
   drawn: a dark cap line? the wall's colour?), or dithered; how the transition looks as the camera orbits (instant or a 0.2 s fade); what the
   floor/skirting does under a cut wall. Reference The Sims 4 walls-cutaway, Two Point Hospital, Prison Architect, Jagged Alliance 3.
2. DOORS: per room (office: wood; physio: white clinical with a push plate; reception: glazed? the gym's front door?) - leaf style, frame
   width and colour (hex), handle, a small sign/plate, standing OPEN at ~100 degrees against the inside wall so paths stay clear; how a door
   reads when its wall is cut away (keep the frame? fade with the wall?).
3. The near-floor edge: what the bottom of a room still should show instead of a dark slab (the corridor floor? a clean edge?).
Give hex colours and sizes in metres. Say what to avoid.

message.content:
**1. Cutaway: cut the near walls down to a stub with a dark cap line, not fade them**

Cut every wall between the camera and the room down to a stub. Don't fade it or dither it. Here's why:
- A faded wall at any alpha still puts a coloured veil over the room, and the brick or tile texture ghosts over the floor. At a 55 to 65° view that veil covers most of the frame, which is exactly the operator's complaint.
- Dithering shimmers when the camera orbits and at phone scale, and it looks like a rendering bug in a bright, clean art style.
- A stub keeps the room's footprint readable (you can see where the wall was and where the doorway is) while hiding nothing inside.

**Spec**
- **Stub height:** 0.40 m above the finished floor. That's just above the skirting and below a seated person's knee, so furniture against the wall still reads. Every room uses the same height, so the building reads as one cut.
- **The cut top edge:** a flat cap the full thickness of the wall, filled with a dark, desaturated colour: #2B2522 (warm charcoal, so it sits with the brick and wood). Add a thin 0.01 m lip line on the room side in the wall's own colour, so the cap belongs to that wall.
  - That's the read used by The Sims 4 and Two Point Hospital: the cut is clearly a cut, not a short wall.
  - Don't show brick or plaster texture on the cap. A flat fill reads cleanly from above.
- **Which walls cut:** any wall whose outward normal faces the camera within about 100° (the walls between the camera and the room's centre). Side walls that run away from the camera stay full height, so you keep two full walls framing the room, like a stage set.
- **Transition while orbiting:** a 0.2 s ease (smoothstep) between full height and the stub, driven by height, not alpha. Animate the top down, or swap at the midpoint with a vertical clip that slides. Don't make it instant: an instant pop on every orbit tick reads as flicker. No continuous motion once settled.
  - Add hysteresis: cut at 100° and restore only at 110°, so a wall at the boundary doesn't flip back and forth.
- **Floor and skirting under a cut wall:** the floor runs right up to the wall line. The skirting stays on the room side at its real height (0.10 m), so it sits inside the 0.40 m stub and reads intact. The parquet, checker or tile ends cleanly at the wall line; it never pokes through.
- **Wall-mounted items on a cut wall** (frames, shelves, whiteboards, a clock): hide anything above the stub height during the cut. Don't leave it floating in the air.

**Mode switch (optional, recommended):** give the player a cutaway toggle with three states: walls up, walls cut (the default), and walls down (floor-level stubs, 0.10 m). This is the Sims convention and players expect it.

**References and what to copy**
- **The Sims 4:** copy the walls-cutaway mode with its short stubs and dark caps, plus the three-state toggle. This is our main model.
- **Two Point Hospital:** copy the clean, bright, stylised look of the cut and how rooms read as boxes with clear doorways from above. The exact way it cuts walls is NOT VERIFIED from here; I'm citing it for the overall read.
- **Prison Architect:** copy the clarity of a pure top-down floor plan as the extreme. It confirms floor and door legibility matter more than walls. It's 2D, so copy only the readability goal, not the technique.
- **Jagged Alliance 3:** copy the roof and wall hiding around the area in focus, keeping far walls standing for context. I haven't checked its exact cut height or fade, so treat that as NOT VERIFIED.

**2. Doors: open at about 100° against the inside wall, with the frame always kept**

General rules:
- Standard leaf size is 0.90 m wide and 2.10 m high, with a 0.04 m thick leaf.
- The frame (casing) is 0.07 m wide on each face, and the threshold strip is 0.02 m high.
- Each door stands open at 100°, swung into the room and resting against the inside wall, so the walking path through the doorway stays a clear 0.90 m.
- Hinges go on the side that puts the open leaf flat against the nearest wall, never into the path.
- When a door's wall is cut, the frame cuts at the stub height (0.40 m) like the wall, with the same cap colour. The open leaf, standing inside the room, stays full height if its wall isn't cut, so the door still reads as a door.
  - If the leaf sits against a wall that's being cut, cut the leaf to the stub height too, with a cap in the leaf's own colour, not the wall cap colour. That way you can still see which object it is.
- Never use a pale see-through panel as a stand-in: every doorway has a real frame and leaf.

**Office: panelled wooden door**
- Leaf: a 4-panel wooden door in a stained medium oak, #7A5230, with a satin finish. The raised panels are 0.01 m proud, with a highlight edge one shade lighter, #9A6B42.
- Frame: dark walnut #4A3220, 0.07 m. This is darker than the leaf so it reads against the wood panelling, which should sit between the two (about #6B4A2E).
- Handle: a brass lever, #B8892E, at 1.05 m. Use a slightly brighter brass so it catches the light.
- Sign: a small brass plate 0.20 × 0.06 m at 1.55 m height, reading "OFFICE" (EXAMPLE string; Kalli owns the words).

**Physio: white clinical door with a push plate**
- Leaf: flush (flat), white with a slight warm tint, #F2F1EC, so it doesn't clip to pure white under bright light.
  - A narrow vision panel 0.15 × 0.70 m, set off-centre at eye height, frosted glass at #CFE3E8 with 60% opacity.
  - A kick plate 0.25 m high at the bottom, in brushed steel #A9AEB3.
- Frame: pale grey steel, #C9CDD1, 0.05 m. It's slimmer and clinical, with a crisp edge against the white tiles.
- Hardware:
  - A push plate 0.10 × 0.30 m in brushed steel at 1.10 m on the push side.
  - A D-shaped pull handle 0.30 m long on the pull side.
- Sign: a white plate with a simple dark-grey pictogram and "PHYSIO" (EXAMPLE), 0.20 × 0.20 m, at 1.55 m.
  - Don't use a red cross. It's a protected symbol, and red reads as an alert in our UI language.

**Reception: the gym's front door, glazed**
- Leaf: a full-glazed door in a slim black aluminium frame. Glass at #DDE7EA, about 30% opacity, with a soft highlight streak. The frame is #1F1F1F, with 0.06 m stiles and a 0.18 m bottom rail.
- Size: a pair of leaves, 0.90 m each, for 1.80 m in total. It's the main entrance and should feel like one.
  - The doors stand open at 100°, pinned back against the outer wall. If the inside wall gets in the way, open them out onto the street side.
- Hardware: long vertical bar handles, 0.60 m, in brushed steel #A9AEB3.
- Sign: the gym name as vinyl lettering on the glass at 1.40 m, white #F4F4F2 (the name is EXAMPLE), plus a small opening-hours decal below it. A hanging "OPEN" sign is optional.
- The checker floor runs right out to the threshold, where a 1.20 × 0.80 m coir doormat sits, #8A6A45. This marks the gym's front door from above in one glance.

**Inner doors between rooms and the training floor (if any)**
- Use a simple flush door in a mid grey-blue, #5E6B78, with a steel frame, so it's clearly a service door and the three hero doors stand out.

**3. The near-floor edge: show the corridor floor, not a dark slab**

The bottom of the frame should show a strip of whatever floor is outside the room. Usually that's the corridor or the training floor, with the cut wall's stub and cap running across it. That puts the room in its building, the way The Sims and Two Point Hospital frame rooms.
- **Strip depth:** at least 1.5 m of corridor floor in front of the near wall, visible in the camera's default framing. Raise or tilt the default camera if needed to get this.
- **The corridor floor:** a neutral surface that doesn't compete with the room floors. Use polished concrete at #8C8780, or the training floor's rubber matting if the room opens onto it (match the S206 zone mat colours).
- **Lighting:** the corridor is about 20% darker than the room's interior, never black. The eye should go into the room, but the corridor still reads as a real place.
- **Edge of the building:** if the room sits on the outer wall, the bottom of the frame shows the outside. For the office, that's the pavement at #9A958C with a kerb, plus the red-brick outer wall as a stub with a cap. Never leave a void.
- **The dark slab is most likely the underside or side of the floor geometry, or an uncut outer wall seen from above.** Kill the slab: give the level edge a clean face in the floor colour, or simply extend the corridor geometry past the frame edge so the camera never sees the end of the world.

**What to avoid**
- **Alpha-faded walls:** a veil of brick or tile over the room.
- **Dithered or stippled walls:** they shimmer when the camera orbits and at small sizes.
- **Instant pops on cut and restore:** use the 0.2 s ease with hysteresis.
- **Continuous motion on walls or doors:** no pulsing outlines or bobbing.
- **Floating objects:** wall-mounted items left in the air above a cut wall.
- **Bare doorways or pale see-through panels** pretending to be doors.
- **Doors swinging into the walking path,** or into the camera's line of sight.
- **Pure white (#FFFFFF) or pure black (#000000) surfaces:** they clip under bright light and lose detail.
- **A red cross on the physio door.**
- **Teal anywhere in the set:** it's reserved for the UI.
- **Black voids at the edge of the frame:** always show a floor.

All hex values are starting points to check under our warm key light in-engine. All signage text is EXAMPLE pending Kalli. I can mock the three rooms with the cutaway, doors and corridor strip as stills if you want to see it before it's built.

# CLIPREVIEW1 - review our boxing fight motion (FightCamp, S259)

FightCamp is a PC boxing-gym management sim: you train a boxer, book his fight, and WATCH the bout as a 3D simulation (two
MetaHuman-style boxers, red trunks vs blue trunks, game camera high and three-quarter, like a broadcast). The operator watched our
latest fight clip and said: "The 3d fight looks terrible torso twists weird legs fly not walk" and "the jab fires like bullet why is
it so fast". We changed the motion system (one writer moves each body per frame instead of eight) and need every reviewer's eyes.

## The clip, in numbers (seed 95501, 40 s, 1,200 frames per boxer; left = before, right = after the change)
| measure | before red/blue | after red/blue |
|---|---|---|
| frames a PLANTED foot slides on the canvas | 315 / 333 | 186 / 161 (13-15%; goal <= 5%) |
| body root moving > 4 m/s (teleport-like) | 8 / 9 | 0 / 0 |
| body root moving > 1.5 m/s | 231 / 229 | 140 / 66 |
| hips lower than 0.70 m (crouched) | 159 / 39 | 116 / 5 |
| feet more than 0.95 m apart | 42 / 44 | 25 / 29 |
| torso twist > 50 deg (red) | 17 | 19 |
| centre-to-centre distance the engine holds in exchanges | 0.557 m - torsos visibly merge | same |

What the frames (every 2 s) show after the change: the red boxer often crouches with bent knees and leans forward into the blue
man; in exchanges the two torsos touch or overlap; bare feet; gloves red; the blue man stands taller and more upright.
The jab: from guard to full extension the glove travels in a very short time - the operator says it "fires like a bullet".

## Questions (answer every one, as long and specific as you can)
1. Which reads more like two real boxers - and where exactly does the motion break (feet, hips, torso twist, spacing)?
2. Feet: real boxing footwork is push-step, pivot, shuffle - never a glide. What should planted feet do during a punch? When must
   a foot move, and how far, in a real jab, cross, hook? Give numbers where you know them.
3. Punch speed: real numbers for an elite and an amateur boxer - jab fist peak speed (m/s), time from guard to full extension (s),
   time back to guard, and how this changes for cross, hook, uppercut. How fast should a VIDEO GAME show it so it reads well to a
   viewer (games often slow punches down - which ones do, by how much)?
4. Spacing: what distance between the two boxers' chest centres in an exchange (jab range, hook range, clinch)? What stops
   torsos merging in fighting games (collision capsules, push-out, animation spacing)?
5. Name the three most important things to fix first, in order, and what a fighting-game animator would do about each.

## Your angle
MARIA (art direction): silhouette, posture, stance width, crouch depth, the broadcast camera, how the two boxers should look side by side so the viewer reads a boxing match at a glance.

Write the longest complete answer you can. Plain words, numbers with units, sources where you have them.

message.content: I'm on the fight-motion review now. First I'm pulling sourced numbers on punch speed, footwork and spacing, so the speeds and distances aren't guesses, and then I'll write the full answer from the art-direction side.
I'll send the full review once the sourced numbers are in.

**1. Which reads more like two real boxers, and where the motion breaks**

The "after" clip is the better one, and the blue boxer is the closer of the two to a real fighter. The teleporting is gone (zero frames above 4 m/s). Blue stands at boxing height (only 5 frames below 0.70 m) and moves more calmly (66 frames above 1.5 m/s, against red's 140). It still doesn't read as a boxing match from the broadcast camera, and here's why, in order of how much each hurts the picture:

- **Spacing.** At a 0.557 m chest-to-chest distance, two adult chests are almost touching. A typical chest is roughly 0.25 to 0.30 m deep, so the gap between them is about 0.25 to 0.30 m. That's my estimate, not sourced. Add red's forward lean and the torsos overlap. From a high three-quarter camera, merged torsos turn two boxers into one blob, and that kills the read before anything else gets a chance.
- **Red's posture.** 116 frames with the hips below 0.70 m means a deep, knees-bent crouch, plus a lean into blue. Real boxers punch from a moderate knee bend. Dinu & Louis (2020) measured knee angles of about 142 to 147° at impact, with the body's centre of mass about 0.9 m up ([Dinu & Louis 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7739747/)). Red's silhouette reads as a wrestler shooting for the legs, not a boxer.
- **Feet.** 13 to 15% of planted frames slide, so the feet glide over the canvas. That's what the operator means by "legs fly, not walk".
- **Torso twist.** More than 50° on 19 frames isn't wrong in itself, because a hook or cross rotates the shoulders a lot. It looks weird when the shoulders twist while the hips and feet don't follow. Real rotation runs up from the ground: rear foot, then hips, then shoulders, then arm. Cheraghi et al. (2014) found the ankle, knee and elbow start extending at about 45%, 60% and 80% of the punch cycle ([Cheraghi 2014](https://aassjournal.com/article-1-136-en.pdf)). A torso that twists on its own, with planted, sliding feet, reads as a broken spine.
- **Stance width.** Feet more than 0.95 m apart on 25 to 29 frames is too wide for most boxers. A boxing stance is about shoulder width or slightly wider ([myboxingcoach](https://www.myboxingcoach.com/stance-and-on-guard/)). For a typical adult man that's roughly 0.45 to 0.65 m, which is my estimate. Over 0.95 m is a lunge.

**What the two should look like side by side (art direction)**
- **Silhouette:** two upright, slightly bent figures in a bladed stance (lead shoulder towards the opponent, about 30 to 45° side-on), chins tucked, and gloves up at the cheekbones. Two clear vertical shapes with a visible gap of canvas between them.
- **Height:** both heads at roughly natural height minus 5 to 10 cm for the knee bend. If one boxer is consistently a head lower, the viewer reads it as a mismatch or a knockdown.
- **Lean:** the spine leans forward 10 to 15° from vertical at most during a punch. It never folds at the hips into the opponent.
- **Broadcast camera:** at a high three-quarter angle, put the gap between the two boxers across the frame, not along the camera's line of sight, so the canvas between them is always visible. If the camera looks straight down the line between the two fighters, they overlap on screen even when they're apart in the 3D scene.
- **Colour:** bare feet and red gloves on both boxers throw away an easy read. Both should wear the Hightops boots and kit colours from M43, with gloves in each boxer's own kit colour, so the eye can follow each boxer's hands.

**2. Feet: what planted feet do in a punch, and when a foot must move**

A planted foot never slides. It can do three things:
- Stay locked.
- Pivot on the ball of the foot, with the heel turning and lifting while the ball stays put.
- Lift and step to a new spot, landing and locking again.

Anything else is a glide.

**What the research says:**
- In a jab, the rear leg pushes. Stanley et al. (2018) measured peak ground force of about 0.63 N/kg on the lead foot against 1.56 N/kg on the rear in the jab. In the cross it was 1.06 against 1.21. ([Stanley 2018](https://chesterrep.openrepository.com/server/api/core/bitstreams/3e769a4f-d46b-4921-a2e9-093e0a80e436/content))
- In the cross, weight moves forward. Elite boxers at impact had about 60% of their vertical force on the lead foot and 40% on the rear. In the hook it was about 59/41, and in the uppercut about 50/50 (Dinu & Louis 2020).
- In a rear straight punch, the hips move about 28 cm towards the target, and the ankle and knee extend by about 12° and 25°, which is the leg drive (Cheraghi 2014).
- I found no study with step lengths, the rear heel's pivot angle in the cross, or the lead foot's pivot in the hook. Treat the numbers below as animator starting points, NOT VERIFIED.

**Per punch (starting points to tune by eye)**
- **Standing jab:** both feet locked. The weight shifts slightly forward through the rear leg's push; the feet don't move.
- **Stepping jab:** the lead foot lifts a few centimetres and steps forward about 15 to 25 cm. The step lands at the same moment as the punch or just before it. The rear foot then slides up by the same distance, a push-step that lifts rather than drags. That lift is what separates it from a glide: the rear foot leaves the canvas.
- **Cross:** the lead foot stays locked. The rear heel lifts and turns outward 45 to 90° on the ball of the foot, with the ball pinned in place. The rear knee turns in, and the hips rotate before the shoulders.
- **Lead hook:** the rear foot stays locked. The lead heel lifts and the lead foot pivots inward on the ball, roughly 45 to 90°, with the knee turning in the direction of the punch.
- **Uppercut:** both feet stay locked. The punching side's knee bends then extends, so the power comes from the legs, and the heel on that side can lift slightly.
- **Footwork between punches:** a small step-and-slide, 10 to 30 cm per step. The foot nearest the direction of travel moves first: the lead foot when moving forward, the rear foot when moving back. The feet never cross, and the stance width comes back after every step.

**Your 5% target and the slide measure.** Check how your sliding number is defined before chasing 5%. In NVIDIA's Kimodo benchmark, a foot counts as sliding while it's on the floor (toe below 0.05 m) and moving faster than 0.2 m/s. Their sample numbers show even real motion capture scoring about 12 to 14% on that measure ([NVIDIA Kimodo metrics](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/sil/projects/kimodo/docs/benchmark/metrics.html)).
- A pivot moves the heel without moving the ball, so separate "ball of foot moving" from "heel turning". Only the first is a slide.
- I'd set the target on the ball of the foot: under 1 cm of movement per planted step.

The fix is what Ubisoft's motion-matching talk recommends: lock the toe when it barely moves in the source animation ([Clavet, GDC 2016](https://archive.org/download/GDC2016Clavet/GDC2016-Clavet_djvu.txt)). Use foot IK to pin it, and blend only while the foot is in the air.

**3. Punch speed: real numbers and what to show**

**Real fist speeds, peak (m/s)**
- **Stanley 2018 (amateur boxers):**
  - Jab 5.85 ± 0.85
  - Cross 6.97 ± 0.86
  - Lead hook 11.95 ± 1.84
  - Rear hook 11.48 ± 1.90
  - Lead uppercut 10.60 ± 2.30
  - Rear uppercut 11.55 ± 1.72
- **Dinu & Louis 2020, elite versus junior, at impact:**
  - Cross 8.1 versus 8.1
  - Hook 11.2 versus 8.9
  - Uppercut 10.2 versus 7.3
- **Kimm & Thiel 2015:** jab 8.1 ± 1.4 (men) and 6.6 ± 1.6 (women); cross 7.7 ± 1.5 and 5.7 ± 1.5 ([Kimm & Thiel 2015](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proeng.2015.07.232)).
- **Whiting 1988:** peak speeds 6.6 to 12.5 m/s, reached 8 to 21 ms before contact ([Whiting 1988](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3377096/)).

So the jab and cross peak at about 6 to 8 m/s, and hooks and uppercuts at about 10 to 12. Elite boxers are faster than juniors mainly on hooks and uppercuts; on the cross they're about the same.

**Real timing (ms)**
- **From the start of the wind-up to contact (Stanley 2018):**
  - Jab 405 ± 150
  - Cross 495 ± 150
  - Lead hook 657 ± 145
  - Rear hook 586
  - Lead uppercut 627 ± 103
  - Rear uppercut 606 ± 100
- **The visible arm-extension phase is much shorter:**
  - Cheraghi 2014 timed a rear straight at 310 ± 60 ms from fist motion to impact, with the fist travelling about 0.655 m. The elbow's extension phase alone was 105 ± 20 ms.
  - Piorkowski et al. (2011) measured about 223 ± 99 ms for a single maximal cross from the forearm starting towards the target to contact ([Piorkowski 2011](https://knowledge.lancashire.ac.uk/id/eprint/3757/1/piorkowski-et-al-2011-punch-kinematics.pdf)).
- **Return to guard:** NOT VERIFIED. No study I found measures it. Cheraghi notes the return is slower than the throw, and Kimm & Thiel couldn't measure it reliably.
- **Elite against amateur timing:** NOT VERIFIED. No study compares it.

**Why your jab "fires like a bullet"**

A real jab isn't instant. It's about 0.4 s from the first shift of weight, and the arm's final snap is only about 0.1 to 0.2 s. A viewer reads the whole thing: the weight shift, the snap, and the slower return. If our jab is just the snap, guard to full extension with no wind-up and a fast snap back, it reads as a muzzle flash, even if the fist speed is realistic. Please measure our jab's guard-to-extension time and peak glove speed in the clip. I can't see our clip data, so I don't know the current numbers.

**How games show it**
- Street Fighter 6's standing light punch hits after 4 frames, about 67 ms at 60 fps, and takes about 7 frames to recover ([SF6 Ken frame data](https://www.streetfighter.com/6/en-us/character/ken/frame)).
- Tekken 8's generic jab hits on frame 10 (about 167 ms) and lasts 29 frames in total ([Tekken generic movelist](https://wavu.wiki/t/Generic_movelist)).
- These count from the button press, not from a wind-up, so they aren't directly comparable to the studies.
- Fighting games add readability by freezing both characters for a few frames at the moment of contact (hit-stop). Capcom describes typical values of 8, 12 and 16 frames for light, medium and heavy hits, "to give the player a sense of the attack hitting as well as the weight". Capcom also notes that a move that misses "may move so fast that you can barely see it" ([Capcom SF Seminar, Hour 11](https://game.capcom.com/cfn/sfv/column/131545?lang=en)).
- I found no source on how EA's Fight Night times its punches, or on broadcast slow-motion conventions.

**What I'd show (art-direction targets for a watched simulation, NOT VERIFIED; tune by eye)**
- **Jab, about 0.40 s in total:**
  - About 80 to 120 ms of anticipation: the weight shifts forward and the shoulder starts to turn.
  - About 100 to 150 ms of extension.
  - About 30 to 50 ms holding at full extension.
  - About 150 to 250 ms back to guard, slower than the throw.
  - That keeps the true peak speed (about 6 to 8 m/s) but gives the eye a beginning and an end.
- **Cross, about 0.50 to 0.55 s:** a longer anticipation, with the rear heel pivot and hips leading. Hold 40 to 60 ms, return 200 to 250 ms.
- **Hooks and uppercuts, about 0.60 to 0.70 s:** a visible load-up in the knees and hips, a fast whip in the middle (the glove is faster than a jab, about 10 to 12 m/s), and a heavier return.
- **On contact:** freeze both bodies for 2 to 4 frames on a clean hit (about 33 to 67 ms), and 0 to 1 frame on a blocked or glancing one. That's a much lighter version of Capcom's hit-stop. We're a watched simulation, not a fighting game, so the freeze is for weight, not for player timing.
- **Don't slow the punch itself into slow motion.** Keep real speed in the middle of the move and add the time to the anticipation, the hold and the return. Slow motion is for replays only.

**4. Spacing: chest-to-chest distances and how games stop torsos merging**

**What's sourced**
- A lab dodge study set attacker-to-target distances of 75, 85 and 95 cm, chosen to sit just beyond the attacker's fully extended arm ([Rev. Psicol. Deporte 2017](https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/revpsidep/revpsidep_a2017v26n2/revpsidep_a2017v26n2p87.pdf)).
- In a rear straight punch, the lead foot ends about 0.50 m from the target (Cheraghi 2014).
- I found no sourced clinch distance and no average reach. Arm span is roughly equal to height.

**What I'd use: chest-centre to chest-centre (my estimates from arm length plus torso depth, NOT VERIFIED; tune in-engine)**

| Range | Chest-centre to chest-centre | What it looks like |
|---|---|---|
| Outside, out of range | 1.4 to 1.8 m | Clear canvas between them, feeling each other out |
| Jab range | 1.1 to 1.3 m | Arm's length plus a step; the jab just lands |
| Hook and uppercut range | 0.7 to 0.9 m | Close, but a visible gap between the chests |
| Clinch | 0.35 to 0.50 m | Chests touch or nearly touch, with heads to one side |

At 0.557 m, the engine is holding everything in clinch range. The two boxers should only be that close when they're actually clinching.

**How fighting games stop bodies merging**
- **Street Fighter's collision box:** a box on the body, without the arms and legs, that exists "to keep two characters from overlapping". Walking into the other character pushes them back, and when special moves end overlapped, the two are separated sideways ([Capcom SF Seminar, Hour 7](https://game.capcom.com/cfn/sfv/column/131422?lang=en)).
- **Pushback on hit or block:** the defender slides back further for heavier attacks. In the corner, the attacker moves back instead ([Capcom SF Seminar, Hour 11](https://game.capcom.com/cfn/sfv/column/131545?lang=en)).
- **EA's Fight Night Round 4:** built on physics, with full-body collision between the two boxers, punches that re-aim based on how close the boxers are, iterated collision volumes, and a dedicated clinch tie-up ([GameSpot, Fight Night Round 4](https://www.gamespot.com/articles/fight-night-round-4-the-physics-of-fighting/1100-6233939/)).

**What I'd do for us**
- Give each boxer a torso capsule about 0.30 to 0.35 m in diameter, from hip to shoulder height, plus a head sphere. Arms don't get capsules. Never let the two torso capsules overlap.
- Instead of a hard push, give each range a preferred distance (from the table) that the simulation steers towards with footwork steps. That way the boxers step back to range, which matches the feet fix, rather than being shoved apart by physics.
- Make the punch reach the opponent, not the other way round. Pick the punch from the current distance, and make small IK adjustments to the arm, a few centimetres, so the glove lands on target. Don't move the body forward to make a punch connect.
- Treat the clinch as its own state with its own animation, where chest contact is allowed and expected.

**5. The three things to fix first, in order**

**1. Spacing and torso collision.** Merged torsos make two boxers unreadable from the broadcast camera before anything else is visible.
- An animator would add body capsules with a no-overlap rule and set preferred distances per range.
- The punch would be chosen from the current distance, and IK on the arm would land it.
- The clinch would be a separate state with contact allowed.
- Red's forward lean would be capped at about 10 to 15° and the crouch limited (hips not below about 0.80 m outside of defensive ducks), so red stands like blue.
- **Success means** chest centres stay at or above 0.70 m apart outside the clinch, and canvas is visible between the boxers on every frame.

**2. Planted feet.**
- Lock the ball of the foot with IK whenever the source animation's foot is nearly still.
- Let pivots rotate the foot around its ball.
- Allow foot moves only as lift-step-land, with the foot clearly off the floor.
- Keep stance width between about shoulder width and 1.5× shoulder width, recovering after each step.
- Fire the pivot from the feet up, so the torso can't twist past the hips.
- **Success means** the ball of a planted foot moves less than 1 cm, and stance width never goes above about 0.75 m outside a deliberate lunge.

**3. Jab timing, and every punch's anticipation and recovery.**
- Keep the real snap speed (about 6 to 8 m/s for the jab) but add a visible wind-up: weight shift, shoulder turn and the rear foot pushing.
- Hold briefly at full extension and slow the return.
- Hit-stop is 2 to 4 frames on a clean hit only.
- Scale the cross, hooks and uppercuts up from there.
- **Success means** a viewer at 1080p and on a phone can name each punch as it happens, and the operator stops calling the jab a bullet.

Once those three are in, the remaining things are presentation: the Hightops boots, kit-coloured gloves from M43, and camera framing that puts the canvas gap between the boxers across the frame. Those are quick wins that make the match read at a glance. The research notes behind every number are saved on my computer at `/workspace/clipreview1/research.md`; I can copy them to Beast if you want them next to this review.

# ASK (Maria, art direction) - make our MetaHuman boxers look real in Godot 4.7 on a broadcast-style fight camera (S262)

Longest complete answer you can. Numbers, not adjectives: every recommendation names the Godot material/light property and a
value or range, and why.

## Context
FightCamp is a boxing manager sim (PC, Steam EA). The fight is WATCHED from a TV-broadcast camera: high, 3/4 view, both boxers
head to feet in frame (they are ~350-450 px tall on a 1920x1080 frame). Bodies are MetaHumans exported from UE 5.8 to Godot
4.7.2 (Forward+): body + head meshes, albedo/normal JPGs (2K), a skin micro-normal, hair and brows as CARDS (no strands),
StandardMaterial3D. Ring lit by four broadcast fills from the truss corners (S261) + a key. The operator (40 years of games):
"the MH models do not look very nice or real to me". Our honest read: Unreal's MetaHuman look comes from its skin shader
(subsurface scattering, dual-lobe specular, cavity/AO), strand/groom hair and Epic lighting - we have none of that in Godot.

## Questions
1. Skin in Godot 4.7 StandardMaterial3D for dark and light skin tones at THIS camera distance: subsurface_scattering_strength,
   subsurf_scatter_skin_mode, transmittance (on/off, depth, color), roughness (value + a roughness map?), specular / metallic_specular,
   clearcoat for sweat (yes/no, value), rim (rim, rim_tint) - and whether a custom ShaderMaterial (dual-lobe specular, cavity
   multiply) is worth it at 400 px tall. Give a recommended starting preset per skin tone.
2. Sweat/oil sheen that builds over rounds (fighters glisten under ring lights) - which property to animate and its range.
3. Hair/brows as cards: alpha mode (alpha scissor vs hash vs depth prepass), anisotropy, how to keep short boxer haircuts from
   looking like a helmet. Should most boxers have shaved/short hair to dodge the problem? (art direction call)
4. Lighting for a believable TV fight look: key/fill/rim ratios, colour temperature, shadow softness, SSAO/SSIL/SDFGI or not,
   tonemap (AgX/ACES/Filmic) and exposure, a touch of bloom on the canvas glare? Name the Environment and Light3D settings.
5. Reference: name 3 shipped games or broadcast stills whose fighter look we should match at this camera height, and what
   each does right (e.g. Undisputed, Fight Night Champion, UFC 5 - what makes their skin read as skin from far away).
6. A "look test" plan: which 4 stills (same pose, same camera) the operator should compare to pick a direction.

Answer as text; we will build the A/B stills from it and the operator picks.

message.content: I'm writing the full Godot look spec now: skin presets per tone, sweat, hair cards, the broadcast light rig, references and a four-still A/B plan.

**The short answer**

At 350 to 450 px tall, a boxer's face is only about 45 to 60 px high (a head is roughly 1/7.5 of body height). At that size, nobody reads pores, micro-normals or strand hair. Skin reads as skin from four things:
- **Correct specular strength and roughness:** a soft, wide sheen, not plastic, not chalk.
- **A soft light-to-shadow edge** on the body, where scattering helps.
- **Believable contact shadows** in the eyes, under the chin, the armpits and under the gloves.
- **Light that looks like TV:** overhead, even, slightly warm, with a rim off the crowd.

Godot's StandardMaterial3D can do all four. The cheapest big wins are not in the skin shader at all: a project-wide limit on shimmering highlights, baked-in brows, short haircuts and the light rig.

All property names below are the Godot 4 `BaseMaterial3D`, `Environment` and `Light3D` API as documented for 4.x. Confirm each in the 4.7.2 inspector before building. If a name has moved, the meaning stays the same.

---

**1. Skin**

**Why `metallic_specular` matters most**

Godot turns `metallic_specular` into base reflectance as F0 = 0.16 × specular². The default of 0.5 gives F0 = 0.04, which is plastic. Real skin is about F0 = 0.028, which works out to `metallic_specular` = 0.42. Set it to 0.40 to 0.42 on every skin material. That alone takes away much of the "rubber doll" look. Keep `metallic` = 0.

**Light skin preset**

| Property | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `metallic_specular` | 0.42 | Skin reflectance, as above |
| `roughness` | 0.55 (range 0.50–0.60) | A wide, soft sheen. Below 0.45 skin looks wet even when dry. |
| `roughness_texture` | Yes. Pack a greyscale mask from the MetaHuman roughness/cavity data if exported; otherwise paint: T-zone (forehead, nose) 0.45, cheeks and body 0.55, lips 0.40, elbows and knees 0.65 | Breaks up the sheen so it isn't one uniform plastic shell |
| `subsurf_scatter_enabled` | true | Softens the edge between light and shadow |
| `subsurf_scatter_skin_mode` | true | Skin-specific red falloff |
| `subsurf_scatter_strength` | 0.45 (range 0.35–0.60) | Above 0.6 the body goes waxy at this distance |
| `subsurf_scatter_transmittance_enabled` | false by default; test true | Only visible on ears and fingers lit from behind, so tiny at 400 px. It's a "B" test, not a default. |
| If transmittance is on | `subsurf_scatter_transmittance_color` about #C2452E, `subsurf_scatter_transmittance_depth` 0.10–0.20, `subsurf_scatter_transmittance_boost` 0.0–0.1 | Red ears when the rim light is behind the head |
| `clearcoat_enabled` | true | Used as a cheap second specular layer (see below) |
| `clearcoat` | 0.10 when dry | A faint tight highlight on cheekbones and shoulders |
| `clearcoat_roughness` | 0.35 | Tighter than the base layer, so the two read as two |
| `rim_enabled` | true | Lifts the body's outline off the dark crowd |
| `rim` | 0.15 (range 0.10–0.25) | Above 0.3 it looks like a glowing outline |
| `rim_tint` | 0.6 | Mixes the rim towards the skin colour rather than white |
| `ao_enabled` | true, with the MetaHuman AO or cavity map if exported | Darkens creases (armpits, the gap between fingers, ears) |
| `ao_light_affect` | 0.3–0.5 | Makes the AO show under direct light too, not just in shadow |
| `normal_scale` | 1.0 on the body normal map | |
| Detail (micro) normal | Off by default (`detail_enabled` false) | At 50 px faces it only adds sparkle and shimmer (see the project setting below) |

**Dark skin preset** (differences only)

| Property | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `roughness` | 0.48 (range 0.42–0.55) | Dark skin is shaped mainly by its highlights, so they need to be a bit tighter and clearer. High roughness on dark skin is what makes it look ashy and grey. |
| `metallic_specular` | 0.42 | Same reflectance; physics doesn't change with skin tone |
| `subsurf_scatter_strength` | 0.30 (range 0.25–0.40) | Melanin absorbs more light, so visible scattering is weaker. Too much turns dark skin muddy or orange. |
| Transmittance colour, if on | about #8A2E22 | Deeper, less saturated red |
| `clearcoat` | 0.12 dry | A slightly stronger second highlight to model the face |
| `rim` / `rim_tint` | 0.20 / 0.5 | Dark skin against a dark crowd needs the outline more |
| Albedo check | Make sure the darkest skin albedo isn't crushed: no main skin area below about sRGB 40/255 (#282828 brightness) | Below that, lighting can't shape it at all and the face turns into a hole |

Medium tones sit between the two: roughness 0.52 and scatter strength 0.38.

**Project settings to set once (these matter as much as the material)**
- `rendering/anti_aliasing/screen_space_roughness_limiter/enabled` = true, `amount` 0.25, `limit` 0.18. This stops sharp highlights from crawling and sparkling on small, distant shapes. It's the main fix for "plastic shimmer" at 400 px.
- `rendering/environment/subsurface_scattering/subsurface_scattering_quality` = 1 (low) or 2 (medium). Medium is enough at this distance.
- `rendering/environment/subsurface_scattering/subsurface_scattering_scale`: start at the default and tune down if the scatter blurs the whole body. It works in screen terms. NOT VERIFIED for 4.7; test it at the broadcast camera.
- Anti-aliasing: MSAA 4× (`rendering/anti_aliasing/quality/msaa_3d`) plus TAA or FSR2 if the project already uses it. Hair and gloves need it.
- Texture import: re-import the normal maps from lossless sources (PNG, not JPG) with Compress Mode set to VRAM Compressed and Normal Map set to Enable (BC5/RGTC). JPG compression on normals shows up as blotchy shading on the body. Mipmaps on for everything.

**Is a custom ShaderMaterial worth it at 400 px tall?**

Not for dual-lobe specular or cavity multiply. Clearcoat already gives a second, tighter highlight on top of the base, which is effectively dual-lobe. Cavity detail is smaller than a pixel at this distance, and AO with `ao_light_affect` covers it.

It is worth it for one reason only: per-boxer sweat driven from the game. A `StandardMaterial3D` can be shared, so changing it on one boxer changes everyone. Convert the skin material to a ShaderMaterial (Godot can convert it in the editor), and add an `instance uniform float sweat` plus a painted sweat mask. Each boxer then carries his own sweat level without duplicating materials.

---

**2. Sweat and oil sheen over the rounds**

Animate three properties from one sweat value (0 fresh, 1 late rounds):

| Property | Fresh (0) | Late rounds (1) | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `clearcoat` | 0.10 (dry second layer) | 0.45–0.55 | The wet film is a separate, sharper layer on top of the skin |
| `clearcoat_roughness` | 0.35 | 0.15–0.20 | Wet film is glossy |
| `roughness` (base) | 0.55 light / 0.48 dark | 0.45 light / 0.40 dark | The skin under the film gets shinier too, but not as much |

**Curve:** sweat builds fast in round 1, then slowly. For example, 0.35 after round 1, 0.6 after round 4, and about 0.85 to 1.0 by the late rounds. Drop it by about 0.1 between rounds, when the corner towels him off. Change it only between rounds or slowly within one, never in jumps.

**Mask:** sweat isn't even. Paint a greyscale mask that's strong on the forehead, nose, upper lip, neck, chest, shoulders and upper back, and weak on the forearms and shins. Multiply sweat by it. This is only possible with the ShaderMaterial conversion above.

**Don't:**
- Use `metallic` for sweat.
- Push `clearcoat` past 0.6.
- Make the whole body one even mirror.
- Use droplet normal maps. Drops are a few pixels at most and would just sparkle.

Vaseline on the face (cut men apply it) is a slightly stronger clearcoat on the brows and cheekbones, about +0.1, from round 1.

---

**3. Hair and brows as cards**

**Art-direction call: yes, most of the roster should have shaved, buzzed or very short hair.** It's true to the sport (many boxers fight with very short hair) and it removes our weakest asset from the frame. Suggested mix for the 12: about 6 to 7 shaved or buzzed, done as albedo on the scalp with no cards; 3 to 4 short crops on cards; 1 to 2 statement styles (braids, cornrows, a short top or a man bun) to keep the roster varied. All of them are EXAMPLE until the character art team agrees.

**Brows: bake them into the head albedo, no cards.** At 50 px faces a brow is 1 to 2 px tall. Cards there only add sorting problems and shimmer. Paint them into the albedo with a slight darkening in the roughness map. Do the same for stubble and beards on most boxers.

**Settings for the remaining card hair:**
- **Transparency:** `transparency` = Alpha Scissor, `alpha_scissor_threshold` 0.4–0.5, with `alpha_antialiasing_mode` = Alpha to Coverage, which works with MSAA 4×.
  - Scissor writes depth, so cards sort correctly and cast and receive shadows, and alpha-to-coverage softens the hard edges.
  - Alpha Hash dithers, and without TAA it shows a visible noise pattern. Use it only if TAA or FSR2 is on, with `alpha_hash_scale` 1.0.
  - Depth Pre-Pass is for soft, semi-transparent hair with real alpha blending. It sorts badly within one hairstyle, so avoid it for the main mass.
- **Anisotropy:** `anisotropy_enabled` true, `anisotropy` 0.5–0.7, with a flowmap if the cards have consistent UV direction. At 400 px it's a small gain, so it's optional. Do it only if the card UVs already run root-to-tip.
- **Roughness and specular:** `roughness` 0.45–0.55, `metallic_specular` 0.35–0.45. Hair isn't shiny enough to be a mirror at this distance.
- **`cull_mode`:** Disabled (double-sided) on cards. Shade the back faces the same.

**How to keep short card cuts from reading as a helmet:**
- **Scalp underneath:** tint the scalp albedo under the cards to the hair colour, with a soft gradient into skin at the hairline. Gaps between cards then show hair-coloured scalp, not bright skin or a dark hole.
- **Thin the hairline:** the outer row of cards at the forehead and temples should be shorter and more transparent, so there's no hard edge.
- **Break the outline:** no perfectly smooth outer shell. A few cards sticking out slightly change the silhouette.
- **Contact shadow:** a slight AO darkening on the scalp just under the hair mass, in the albedo or AO map, so the hair sits on the head rather than floating above it.
- **Don't** give the hair a strong `rim`. A bright rim on a hair mass is what makes it look like a moulded plastic helmet.

---

**4. Lighting for a TV fight look**

**What a TV fight looks like (art-direction target):**
- Very bright, fairly even light on the ring from above and from the truss.
- Soft but clear shadows under the boxers.
- The ring canvas is the brightest surface in the frame, and the crowd falls into darkness.
- The boxers get a slight rim from the lights behind them.
- It's flatter than a film: the contrast between lit and shadowed sides is low so faces read on every side.

These are my starting values to tune by eye, NOT VERIFIED against measured broadcast rigs.

**Ratios:**
- The key and the combined truss fills should be about 2:1 at the boxers' faces, with the shadow side about one stop darker. That's TV-flat, not dramatic.
- The rim, from the fills behind the boxer relative to the camera, should be about 1.0 to 1.5× the fill.

**The rig:**
- **Key:** an overhead `SpotLight3D` (or `DirectionalLight3D` if the ring is the only thing lit) over the centre of the ring, aimed straight down or up to 15° towards the camera.
  - `light_energy`: set so the canvas reads just under white after tonemapping.
  - `spot_angle` wide enough to cover the ring, 35 to 50°, with `spot_attenuation` low (0.5–1.0) so the light is even across the canvas.
- **Four truss fills (S261):** `SpotLight3D` at about 45° down from the corners, each at about 0.5× the key's energy.
- **Colour temperature:**
  - Default: 4800 to 5200 K, slightly warm white, which reads like a modern LED broadcast with a warmer grade. Put the fills about 300 K cooler than the key so the shadow side reads slightly cool.
  - Option B: the classic warm tungsten look at 3200 to 3600 K.
  - Use `light_temperature` if physical light units are on in the project. Otherwise set `light_color`, about #FFF1E0 for 5000 K and #FFD3A1 for 3400 K.
- **Shadow softness:**
  - `shadow_enabled` true on the key and two fills. Four or more shadowing spots is expensive, so pick the two that face the camera's shadow side.
  - `light_size` 0.25–0.5 m on spots for soft contact shadows (PCSS). Keep `shadow_blur` at about 1.0.
  - Tune `shadow_normal_bias` (about 1.0–2.0) so there's no shadow acne on the skin.
- **`light_specular`:** about 0.5 on the fills and 1.0 on the key, so the skin has one main highlight, not five.

**Environment:**

| Setting | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `tonemap_mode` | AgX (default); Filmic as option B | AgX handles bright light on skin gracefully, without the orange-and-yellow shift that ACES gives skin |
| `tonemap_exposure` | 1.0, tuned so the canvas sits at about 90% brightness | Fixed and stable, like a broadcast camera |
| `tonemap_white` | 6–10 if the tonemapper uses it | Room for the bright canvas |
| Auto exposure | Off | Broadcast exposure doesn't pump |
| `ssao_enabled` | true | Contact shadows in armpits, under the chin and between the boxers |
| `ssao_radius` | 0.5–1.0 | Metre scale; body-sized creases |
| `ssao_intensity` | 1.5–2.0 | |
| `ssao_power` | 1.5 | |

**5. References to match at this camera height**

I can't check how each game's renderer handles skin internally, so these are what to look at in stills, not claims about how they're built.
- **EA Sports UFC 5:** compare its wide broadcast camera stills. Look at how skin keeps a soft, consistent sheen in the overhead octagon light, and how sweat builds over rounds into a stronger highlight on the shoulders and face. That's the sweat model to copy.
- **Undisputed (Steel City):** compare its default TV camera. Look at the warm boxing-ring palette, the bright canvas with a dark crowd, and how the boxers' silhouettes stay clear against it. That's the closest framing to ours.
- **Fight Night Champion (2011):** it's older tech, but its broadcast cameras show that strong, even overhead light plus a good highlight on the shoulders and back reads as skin from far away, even with modest shaders. That's a useful reminder that lighting does most of the work.
- **Real broadcasts (DAZN, ESPN/Top Rank or Sky Sports stills from a wide camera):** the truth reference. Look at the canvas brightness, how dark the crowd is, the overhead shadow under the boxers, and the late-round sweat sheen. Pick 3 or 4 frames and keep them next to the look test.

**6. The look test: four stills**

Use the same frame in all four: both boxers in a neutral guard at jab range (about 1.2 m chest to chest), the broadcast camera at its default height and angle, at 1920×1080.
- One boxer has dark skin and one has light skin, so every still tests both presets.
- One boxer is shaved and one has short card hair.
- Each still also gets a 2× crop of the two heads, from the same render, beside it.

| Still | What changes | What it answers |
|---|---|---|
| **A: Baseline** | What we have today | The starting point |
| **B: Material pass** | Skin presets from section 1, the roughness limiter, baked brows, normal maps re-imported, the current lights | How much the materials alone fix |
| **C: Material + broadcast light** | B plus the section 4 rig: 5000 K, AgX, SSAO, the canvas bounce fake and a touch of glow | Whether it reads as TV |
| **D: Late-round look** | C plus sweat at about 0.85 and SSIL on | Whether sweat sells "skin under ring lights" |

Optional E, if the operator wants a second colour choice: C at 3400 K with Filmic tonemapping, the warm tungsten look. That way the choice between a modern and a classic broadcast look is separate from the material and lighting fixes.

**How to judge:** the operator looks at the full frame first, at 100% and on a phone-size downscale, then at the head crops. Pick the still where both boxers read as people with skin, and the dark-skinned boxer's shape is as clear as the light-skinned one's.

**What to avoid**
- `metallic_specular` at the default 0.5 on skin, or `metallic` above 0.
- Roughness under 0.4 on dry skin.
- Scatter strength above 0.6.
- Detail micro-normals at this camera distance.
- Brow and stubble cards.
- A strong rim on the hair.
- ACES on skin, which shifts it orange and yellow.
- Auto exposure.
- SDFGI.
- Teal anywhere in the ring lighting; it's reserved for the UI.
- Pure black ambient, which turns dark skin into silhouettes in shadow.
- Changing several things between two stills, so you can't tell which one helped.
